Question: About half the nitrogen in your body passed through a factory. Inside a steel reactor, nitrogen from the air meets hydrogen gas at 500 °C. Ammonia forms. But the reactor never turns all of the gas into ammonia. Some nitrogen and hydrogen are always left over. What are the molecules doing that keeps the reaction from going all the way?
Answer: Nitrogen and hydrogen molecules collide and react to form ammonia. At the same time, ammonia molecules break apart into nitrogen and hydrogen again. As ammonia builds up, the reverse reaction speeds up and the forward reaction slows. When the two rates are equal, the amounts stop changing, but both reactions keep running. So some nitrogen and hydrogen are always left.
Target concept: Dynamic equilibrium: forward and reverse rates become equal, amounts stop changing, and the reaction does not go to completion

Question: Astronauts on Mars will need fuel to fly home. A robot fills a sealed steel chamber with carbon monoxide and steam and heats it to 800 K. Hydrogen fuel starts to form. A gas analyzer shows the hydrogen rising, then holding steady, while some carbon monoxide is still inside. The pressure gauge never moves at all. What are the molecules doing once the analyzer reading stops changing?
Answer: Carbon monoxide and water molecules collide and swap atoms to make carbon dioxide and hydrogen. At the same time, carbon dioxide and hydrogen molecules collide and swap back. When the two happen at the same rate, the amounts stop changing, but both reactions keep running. Each swap trades two molecules for two, so the number of molecules, and the pressure, never changes.
Target concept: Dynamic equilibrium: forward and reverse rates become equal, amounts stop changing, and the reaction does not go to completion
